series: HTTPS & TLS: THE HANDSHAKE HANDBOOK — PART 4

blocks.title: Revocation Is Broken
items: CRLs are enormous and rarely fresh
OCSP leaks your browsing to the CA
OCSP fails open — the attacker just blocks it
OCSP stapling: server fetches its own response
Then staples it into the handshake
Fixes both the privacy leak and the latency
`Must-Staple` in the cert makes it non-optional

blocks.title: Expiry Is Winning
blocks.text: Short lifetimes beat revocation infrastructure: a 47-day cert is its own expiry mechanism.

blocks.title: Valid Cert, Wrong Site
blocks.text: A perfectly valid cert for `attacker.com` passes chain validation on a connection to `bank.com`. Only the hostname check catches it.

items: One: is the chain cryptographically valid and trusted
Two: does this cert belong to the host I dialed
Skipping step two is the classic silent vuln
Match SAN ==dNSName== against the URL's host
Not the IP, not the redirect target
Wildcard: leftmost label only, never across a dot
Trailing dots and punycode homographs cause bypasses

caption.text: Part 4 of HTTPS & TLS: THE HANDSHAKE HANDBOOK. The padlock does not mean the site is safe — it means the bytes are encrypted to whoever answered the phone. This handbook walks the TLS 1.2 and 1.3 handshakes packet by packet, decodes certificate chains and SAN matching, explains why SNI still leaks every hostname you visit, and ends with the config checklist and error-triage table you actually reach for at 2am. 10 pages, no fluff: internals, trade-offs, and the misconfigurations that bite in production.
